name: data
label: Data and documents

tools.name: anydoc
tools.use: Convert a document to markdown — Word, PowerPoint, Excel, OpenDocument, RTF, EPUB, CSV or PDF. This is how you open a file someone attached: an attachment is a path under uploads/ and nothing else, so its contents are not in the conversation until you convert it.
tools.args: One or more file paths, relative to the workspace. Prints markdown; redirect through a shell to save it, e.g. ["bash","-lc","anydoc uploads/report.docx > report.md"].

tools.name: mlr
tools.use: Miller: treat CSV, TSV and JSON as records — summarise, filter, cut, sort, join, reshape, and convert between the three. The first tool for a question about a data file.
tools.args: Format flags first, then a verb: --icsv --opprint stats1 -a sum,mean,count -f COLUMN; --icsv --ojson cat; --c2p head -n 5; filter '$qty > 3'; sort -nr qty; join -j id -f other.csv.

tools.name: sqlite3
tools.use: Real SQL. Query a .db/.sqlite file someone attached, or import a CSV first when a question needs joins and grouping beyond what mlr expresses.
tools.args: The database path then SQL, or dot-commands: .tables and .schema to see what is there; -csv for CSV output. Import with ["bash","-lc","sqlite3 d.db '.mode csv' '.import sales.csv sales'"].

tools.name: jq
tools.use: Filter or reshape JSON when the job is smaller than a record pipeline.
tools.args: A jq filter, then a file — or nothing after it to read stdin. -r prints raw strings.

tools.name: yq
tools.use: The same for YAML, and for XML and TOML — config files, CI definitions, OpenAPI documents.
tools.args: A yq expression then a file. -o=json converts to JSON; -p=xml reads XML.

tools.name: file
tools.use: Ask what a blob really is — the first move on any attachment with a vague, wrong or missing extension.

tools.name: 7z
tools.use: List and extract archives and containers — zip, 7z, tar, gz, xz, iso, cab, wim and more. Handles far more formats than unzip, so reach for it when `file` says something unexpected.
tools.args: `l ARCHIVE` lists without extracting, `x ARCHIVE -oDIR` extracts preserving paths, `a OUT.7z PATHS` creates one.

tools.name: strings
tools.use: Pull the printable text out of a binary — the quick way to see what an unknown blob mentions before deciding how to open it.
tools.args: A path. -n N sets the minimum run length (default 4); pipe into rg to search it.

tools.name: exiftool
tools.use: What a file says about itself: camera and GPS for a photo, author and producer for a PDF or a Word file, timestamps for anything.
tools.args: A path to read it. -json for machine-readable output, -s -s -s TAG for one value, -all= to strip every tag.

tools.name: rg
tools.use: Search inside text, CSV and markdown you have saved — find the column, the id, the odd row.
tools.args: A pattern and a path, relative to the workspace. -n prints line numbers, -i ignores case, -c counts.

notes: Identify first: `file` on anything with a vague extension, then `7z l` if it is a container. Convert a document once with `anydoc`, save the markdown, and `rg` the saved file rather than converting again. Sanity-check before summarising — `mlr --c2p head -n 5` and a row count catch a wrong delimiter or a header read as data before either becomes a confident wrong number. Write derived results to files and name them. `tar`, `zip` and `xz` are here too for the cases 7z handles awkwardly. There is no OCR — a scanned PDF has no text layer and converts to nothing, which the web-research toolbox's `doc` command handles instead. Paths are the same ones the file tools use: write `uploads/sales.csv`, not an absolute path.
